Every second day or every third day a certain number of the pieces of ammunition would be given to soldiers, and the rest would go to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was the ammunition physically delivered to the Vinko Skrobo unit? It was at the headquarters, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes, the headquarters in Kalemova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that you were primarily a truck driver, moving various shipments around, delivering shipments to the Kalemova Street headquarters and it's a fact, isn't it, sir, that you know extremely little, if anything, about what happened at the confrontation line, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The child who was killed by the hand grenade, did you ever hear that the soldier who had that hand grenade had pulled the pin on that hand grenade and was rolling it across the floor to the child as if it was some sort of toy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear that. They lived together in the same house. That was in the same room, they slept there, they took their rest there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you're telling this Chamber, sir, that Mr. Martinovic after this event where the child was killed, that Mr. Martinovic threw these soldiers out of the Vinko Skrobo unit; is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes. He called the police to investigate, to check what had happened and told them not to come back. They stayed for another couple of days, until they received their salaries, and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, apart from whatever the military police did or the police did, Mr. Martinovic threw them out or discharged them from his unit, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, when these soldiers were doing whatever it was they were doing with the hand grenade that resulted in the child being killed, were these soldiers on duty at the time? Or were they off duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: That was where they slept in the house, the house that now houses the Croatian embassy. They were not on the line. That was during their leisure time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And yet, sir, for this off-duty conduct, Mr. Martinovic threw them out of the unit, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Mr. Martinovic throw any soldiers out of his units for expelling Muslims from their homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: We only manned the line. I don't know whether anything like that happened. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of Mr. Martinovic throwing any soldiers out of his unit for engaging in looting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I don't know of any such -- I don't know of looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you aware of Mr. Martinovic throwing any soldiers out of his unit because they had abused prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: They never objected, the prisoners. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you don't really know what the prisoners at the confrontation line objected to or not because you weren't at the confrontation line, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were involved in transporting prisoners from the Heliodrom for Stela's unit, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I think so. I think I went once or twice. I can't remember. Dinko did that, and if Dinko couldn't, then anybody else who was free at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were the general truck driver, so wouldn't it be quite logical that if someone needed to drive a truck to the Heliodrom, you would be one of the men to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: It was not just me who could drive a truck. Not -- it was not my truck. I drove my truck. I didn't drive the army truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you drive prisoners from the Heliodrom to the confrontation line in Mostar for any other HVO units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: No. My truck is a big --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't interpret because the witness was speaking English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We didn't get a full answer, Mr. President, I don't know if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, witness, would you please repeat your answer? Because we did not get it. You said no, my truck is a big -- then it stopped. We couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My truck is a big truck, and it couldn't get all the way to the Heliodrom because it was a very winding, dirt road. So it just couldn't be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir in terms of taking prisoners from the Heliodrom, you testified earlier this afternoon, in response to questions from counsel, that you had personal knowledge or familiarity with the forms or orders that were used for taking prisoners from the Heliodrom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately how many times prior to coming to The Hague to testify, how many times had you been involved with those forms, had you filled out a form or signed a form or done any paper work for the taking of prisoners from the Heliodrom to any HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: The orders were issued by the military police. The town defence. Nobody else could do it, to go to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask who could do it. I said how many times -- how many times were you personally engaged in completing such paper work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is it correct, sir, that in fact when you were shown those documents today, you have no personal knowledge to provide this Chamber with at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I never saw a paper from the Heliodrom, the one from the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you other than reading the forms that the papers that were put before you today, other than reading those papers out loud, you have no personal knowledge of those papers or about those papers, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you -- you said a few moments ago that it was Mr. Zlatan Mijo Jelic who was a commander that came most often, I think you said, to Mr. Martinovic's headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I said that I knew him best. Others also came but I didn't know them, so I don't remember them. There were some others from Livno and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, was there some particular relationship between the Mrmak or Vinko Skrobo unit and the unit that was commanded by Mr. Jelic, the military police light assault Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Again, I said that there were Motorolas, the town defence department gave them to everybody, and when an order would be issued, everybody was interconnected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you observe any personal relationship, others than commander, superior-subordinate, between Mr. -- if you contend that's what it was, between Mr. Jelic and Mr. Martinovic? Were they friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Not that I would notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it frequently the case, if you know, that the Stela's unit operated jointly with the Light Assault Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say never, sir, you mean not to your knowledge, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the 17th of September, 1993, you've told the Chamber that you have some personal knowledge of what happened that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know anything that happened on the 17th of September, 1993? In connection obviously with the confrontation line in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I know that there was an attempt to launch an operation, but that this failed through, and that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At any time, sir, on the 17th of September, 1993, were you at the health centre or at the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes. I came once to replace my batteries for the -- for my Motorola. Actually I brought a spare set.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what time of day was it when you went there to replace your battery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I believe it was sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there any fighting going on at the time you went there to change the battery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during the time that you went there to change your battery, how long were you at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So can we properly understand, sir, that any personal knowledge you have of anything that happened at the confrontation line on the 17th of September, 1993, is limited to five minutes when you were there in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall an incident in about the 24th of November, 1993, where Mr. Martinovic's unit and the Baja Kraljevic ATG and Mr. Naletilic, Tuta, and others attacked a military police station in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: On. It's the first time I hear this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I have the usher's assistance to show the witness Exhibit P705.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just for the record, and as a matter of principle, I object to the way the Prosecution works. They always deliver their exhibit at the last moment to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've complied with the Court's orders on all occasions with one or two exceptions when there was an error on the distribution of the documents. I think the Chamber knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at the Croatian version of Exhibit 705.1. Directing your attention to paragraph numbered 1. To avoid any confusion that we had earlier today, sir, I'm going to read this particular portion to you, you can follow along in the first part of paragraph numbered 1 on the first page. "At about 2030 hours on 24 November, 1993, mechanical engineering faculty, in other words the premises occupied by the 1st military police Battalion and the 5th military police Battalion, was invaded by soldiers of the Convicts Battalion, the Vinko Skrobo ATG, the Baja Kraljevic ATG, and former soldiers of Juka under the command of Bozo Sain. They were led by Mladen Naletilic, aka Tuta, who ordered all the members of the military Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. police to lay down their weapons and put them down on the floor." Do you remember this incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have patiently waited for my colleague to read this part of the document, and I object for the simple reason. The witness has already testified that he doesn't know anything about this. So the Prosecution has just used this opportunity to read this document, and that was the sole purpose of the Prosecutor's reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, so far as I know, that this document has already been admitted. I believe that the Prosecution asked a question to this witness, and this witness answered no. Then the Prosecutor is entitled to show him a document, to help the witness to refresh his memory. I don't see anything wrong and at the same time, the witness has the full right to answer this question according to his knowledge. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me probe a moment longer. I think I can finish before the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony to the Chamber that you either -- you did not participate in this event as a member of the Vinko Skrobo unit, and that you never heard of this incident? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I have heard something, but never like this, like it says here. This looks like somebody's private interest. I don't know who all these units were. So many soldiers. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my question. I didn't ask you if you knew all the members of each unit described. My question to you is very simple. Did you participate in this event on the 24th of November, 1993? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you knew of it, didn't you, sir? And you know about it now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I didn't know. I heard something later on, that something had happened, but not so much. There was not so much being said about this. And in the town of Mostar, whenever something happens, you immediately hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: That there was something private, not like this. I don't know who this was. And what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you certainly heard more than that, didn't you? You just told this Chamber you heard something like this. Now you heard more than it was something private. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes. I have not a clue, a private showdown, I don't know between who, but none of us ever went anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My final question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were the logistics officer of this unit, a small unit, which probably never numbered more than about three times the number of persons in this courtroom. You knew most of the members of the unit personally. And you're telling me that you did not hear, there was no one talking about, the soldiers didn't talk about, attacking the military police unit on the 24th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will break and we'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we start, I notice that Mr. Naletilic is absent. Mr. Krsnik, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My client felt sick and he didn't have his nitroglycerine with him so he asked to be taken back to the detention unit, just in case, but we can resume, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. We only hope that your client will have a speedy recovery. Yes, Mr. Seric, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Mr. President. I'd like to ask that the witness be shown once again the order of the 9th of September, 1993. That is Exhibit 551.1, just one page, 01537684. Perhaps we can use my copy. [In English] Yes, okay. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we are going back to this order. In the light of the cross-examination. Did you see, as a logistics man, did you see this order or any order like this there? Will you please speak up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, Mr. Witness, were you the logistics officer or one of the persons with the Vinko Skrobo involved in delivery of necessary supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Well, I was one of the main ones. I had some deputies but I was number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So did that position as logistics officer involve quite a lot of paperwork?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Diarra?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I'd like to ask you a question because I didn't quite understand your answer concerning the state that Nenad Harmandic was in. When you saw him you said that his body was bruised. Did you ask who beat him? I didn't quite get the answer that you gave. That is who it was who beat him and where he came from, and especially when you saw him, was he sitting down or was he working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: I didn't ask him. I asked his colleagues who were with him and they said that he had been brought in that state from the Heliodrom, that that was where he was beaten, and when I saw him he was doing something over the car. He only had on his head some bruises or something. Nothing -- I mean a couple of bruises, a black eye, but he walked normally and all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you saw him working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Yes. He was repairing a car or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of the Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Only a brief clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When asked by Her Honour Judge Clark whether you were the logistics officer in that unit and you answered in the affirmative, so I wanted it to be clear and for the record, were you an officer or a foot soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MT
utterances.text: Well, she asked me whether I was an officer but I said I was just a man, a logistics man a foot soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, thank you, witness, for coming here to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We all wish you a good journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. Thank you. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to tender the photograph marked by the witness, that is where he marked the confrontation line and the barriers. That would be D2/54. Then the order that we covered with the witness, D2/55. And that is the order of the 9th of September, 1993. And it was shown once again. And I also wish to tender the report of the 28th of -- that was the Prosecution's Exhibit 551.1 and our -- it will be our exhibit D2/56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I did not catch you. Would you please repeat the number of the document you are going to tender? I know that the photo originally is numbered as P14.5. The document, that P551.1, and how about another document? Would you please tell me the Prosecution's number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor's number for the last exhibit that we are tendering is P612.1. That is the report of the 28th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to ask Madam Registrar whether this document has been admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P612.1 was tendered under Sir Martin Garrod and it was not admitted, and I will check the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These three documents are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. admitted into evidence. Do you have any documents to tender, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no new exhibits to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So are we going to have the next witness or we break now? What's your suggestion, Mr. Seric, since Mr. Naletilic is not here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd go on. I'd go on. I don't know if anybody else has some other suggestion. Because I believe that there is plenty of time for me even to complete the direct examination of the witness. I mean, he was here yesterday and then he was turned back because of that unfortunate misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the next witness, Mr. Usher? I saw today is the anniversary for the start of the case so we may have an early recess. Any way, we will hear the witness. We still have an hour for us to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Shalom. My greetings to the honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Will you please introduce yourself, to start with, tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Mandelbaum from Mostar, son of Morris and Sarah Finci, they were two inmates in World War II, then they married, they lost their whole families. I have a brother who is two years younger. I am married to a beautiful woman from Dalmacija, her name is Katica. We have four children. I graduated in mechanical engineering and I'm a mechanical engineer. Before the war, I worked for Sokol, and I was the head of the unit assembling installations. I've lived all my life in Mostar. I'm the President of the Jewish community in Mostar. I work now in the department of the ministry for energy and industry in Mostar as the head of the department for industrial entrepreneurship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell this Court where you lived, where you live now, what happened to you in view of your place of residence, today and especially during those unfortunate wartime events in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: On the 4th of April, 1992, after a cistern exploded in front of a high rise building, I lost my flat because my building was demolished. In that 65 other tenants were in that building. There were 65 flats there. And the municipality of Mostar offered us, as a provisional accommodation, in the pensioner's home where I was allotted two rooms, since I have four children. And I lived in that pensioner's home almost for the duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, during that time, where were the premises of the Jewish community in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: The premises of the Jewish community were in my room. That is, in the Ero hotel, whilst I lived there, and later on, where I moved, to the flat of a colleague of mine, who was -- I mean relocated in 1993. I moved over to his flat, which was on Stjepan Radic, 76 D, and that is where the office of the Jewish community in Mostar was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and I'm now referring to the beginning of the war, the first war, the first conflict of the Serb aggressor and the Yugoslav People's Army and the HVO in Mostar, what happened to you, to you personally? What happened to the members of your Jewish community?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Before the war in Mostar, there were 129 members of the Jewish community of Mostar. Today, there are 45 members of the Jewish community. Before the war, the Jews lived on both banks of the Neretva. That is in what is called today east side and west side of Mostar. Today, -- so we lived on both sides, and during this -- sorry, could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes. You are on the right track but let's try to focus on the conflict between the Serb aggressor and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Uh-huh, yes. During the conflict with the Serb aggressor, the office was in the pensioner's home, and that is where I conducted my activities. The first thing that happened is that my brother, somebody came from the military police of the HVO and he was taken away and locked up in Mostar. That was the time when they were around, the people, that is they were rounding up Serbs to exchange them for Croats, I presume who had been captured at that time and so he was looked up in -- in Mostar and I didn't know why he had been detained but I had some friends from before the war who were judges in the district court and I asked them but they couldn't give me an answer. On one occasion when I saw my brother, unloading sandbags, when I saw him unload sandbags I asked him why had he been detained? And he said they were -- accused me of cooperating with the Yugoslav People's Army. Otherwise, he was the head for petrol installations at the Yugo petrol. After that, since I knew that he didn't cooperate I went first to the military police and I believe Stipe Maric, Zeljko Dzidic and I tried to find out, and then I allowed myself to Mr. Jadranko Topic who was the mayor of Mostar. He received me immediately and then he -- and then I saw that as the President of the Jewish community I could do something in the town. So he received me so that my brother was released 10 later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, whatever you say in this courtroom will be translated into the other two languages. We rely on the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, I will speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please make a pause between each sentence so that the interpreter could catch up with you. There is no hurry. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let me lead you a little bit and you will tell us, and wait for me to finish my question and then start answering. Now, you also tell us what was the outcome regarding your brother?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Mr. Topic released him from prison one evening and my brother was in the pensioner's home because his house had also been demolished, together with me, he lived there. On one occasion, when I was in front of the pensioner's home, one of HOS soldiers in a black uniform approached me and asked for my ID, and he read out that my name was Zoran Mandelbaum so he asked me who I was and I said that I was an engineer with Sokol and that I was engaged in the reconstruction of wheat silos in Mostar and he started to take me away and I told him that I worked, that I was not a Serb, and at that moment, on the -- my wife happened on the balcony of the room that we lived in, and she said, "I'm a Croat. I have a domognisa. This is my husband, we live together. Let him go." And he let me go. So I returned -- I went back inside and then I thought what should I do now? Because she told me, well, don't walk around because somebody might get you again, and I knew that if they took me away it will be a question whether I would survive because I was a Jew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you turn to somebody? Did you ask somebody for help in view of the situation that you were in? That you were in and that members of your Jewish community in Mostar were in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Yes. After that, as I said, I thought about it for several days, and I told myself, well, I went through it all once, God knows whether I'll get away another time. There was 60 Jews in -- there were 80 Jews about whom I took care, getting aid from Caritas, Merhamet, the Red Cross, the Jewish community in Split. However, on that occasion, one day, I decided to go to Stela. His residence was in the immediate vicinity of the pensioner's home, and especially as that day, at the gate, there was Meho Mehisa [phoen], one of my welders. He was a guard. And I asked him if I could see Stela. I told him that I was the President of the Jewish community and that I'd like to talk to him. And he went and then came back and told me that he would receive me. So escorted by this, and I believe his name was Semir Bosnjic, who had come there, I went upstairs and there was at a desk, Stela, barefoot. He had his feet on the table. And asked me what I wanted. And I looked him in the eyes, because I felt that if I -- I somehow felt much safer when I looked somebody in the eye and I asked him whether he could tell me what was I to do, that we have had an understanding with Mr. Mate Boban, that is that the state of Israel had established contact with Mr. Mate Boban in London, and on that occasion, Mate Boban had promised to the Jews in the territory of Herceg-Bosna would not suffer any harm, and said that he would order his units to enable the Jews to move unobstructed around Herceg-Bosna and to emigrate to the state of Croatia, that is to Israel or some other third country, and also the passage of Jewish convoys to help Jews who had remained living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to bring them food in. So I told him that, and he then put his feet -- took his feet off the table and there three men standing behind him and there were also three men standing behind me and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he told me to sit down so I did and he asked me what I'd like to drink and I said I didn't care, and then one of these men of his brought me a drink, a whiskey, and offered me whiskey and I picked up this glass, and I thought with a knock our glasses but he hit his glass on the table and I did the same thing. I knocked my glass against the table. And on that occasion, he said, "In the Second World War, Jews paid for everybody else. In this war, there is no need for the -- for anything to happen to the Jews." And I was surprised by this answer because I heard that he'd been a taxi driver before the war, that that was how his way of thinking, and he said that if I had any difficulty, any problem, that if I ran into any difficulty that I should come to him. And I transmitted it all to other members of the Jewish community, since in Mostar, after the holocaust that they survived in 1941 and 1945, all the Jews have been living in mixed marriages so that we have wives and husbands who are Croats and Serbs and Muslims and for that reason, I went to see him, and he instilled a certain security in me, certain confidence, that I could go and turn to him because at that time the official HVO unit was one thing and their unit, the unit in which a number of people turned up, people who could not-- who would have been taken as -- well, not normal but people who acted on their own, and that is why I was afraid of them. However, he instilled certain confidence in me and throughout the war that I spent in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Tell us, now, let us move on to the period after the -- following the 9th of May, which is the key period of time in this case. Following the 9th of May, 1993, that is after the conflict broke out between the BH Army and the Croat Defence Council, tell us what did you do, as the president of the Jewish community? Were you -- did you concentrate only on extending help to members of your community or was it broader? I'm referring to the Croat-Muslim conflict.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I'd nevertheless like to go back a little. I told you that I had established contact with Mr. Topic and that as the President of the Jewish community, I gained some confidence that I could approach them and therefore ask for help for some people. So even prior to the 9th of May, 1993, I was engaged in helping -- in helping my Serb acquaintances who had either been detained in Celovina, in Mostar, or needed some documents to get out in somehow. And for some reason I met with sympathy on the part of the official authorities in Mostar, so the first conflict, that is when Muslims began to be expelled from Mostar, was on the 20th of April, 1993. On that occasion, first the Muslims who were not the domicile population were expelled first. That is those who had arrived from Eastern Herzegovina and then there was a lull for about ten days. And then on the 9th of May, 1993, massive expulsion started and we were all witnesses to it. During that period of time, since I knew who was who in the town, and that the Jewish community was an institution, during that period, I maintained contact only with people who were the highest authorities during that period of time, and I engaged in humanitarian activities. So I communicated with Mr. Slobodan Bozic, through whom I managed to get out some of my friends from the Heliodrom, that is to get the permits for them to leave, through him I also obtained some passes for some other people, that is passes -- I'm referring to Muslims, to get out of Mostar. Also during that period of time I issued some certificates to some people, as if they were members of the Jewish community even though they had Muslim names and with those documents they could enter Croatia, and that saved them. Later on, depending on who came to me and about what, or rather every day, whenever I would get up, I would tell myself I need to do a good deed today. Now, depending who came to me and who turned to me for help. I did -- I would go to the official authorities. I believe I am the only citizen of Mostar, a civilian, who saw the war from both sides of the front line, from the west, from West Mostar, because I was there, and from East Mostar, because I also went to the east side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have to slow down because we have difficulties to follow the translations and the transcript. Mr. Seric, would you please keep the pace?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I know that, sir, you should address the Trial Chamber and that is what you do out of respect, but from time to time, you should look towards me. I will warn you. I'll give you a sign when I think you need to slow down. I know that you respect this Trial Chamber and that you want to tell your story to the Trial Chamber but please pay attention to me.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I wanted to say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Slow down. Let me guide you a little. Can you tell us, how was it possible that you cross the line between the East and West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I wanted to help people. Those people who were persecuted just because much their religion or because of their ethnic background. This was always on my mind. I always recalled how the Jews suffered during the Second World War. Since I saw that ordinary people were against the war, the citizens of Mostar were against the war, they asked after each other. The war was due to the politics and I found a way as to how to cross from one side to another. I established contacts with the highest leading people in Herceg-Bosna, like Mr. Vlado Soljic the Defence Minister, then Perica Jukic, Ante Roso, the two of them were together. And they granted me their approval for me to go to the eastern part of Mostar. With their approval, with their pass, I went to Medjugorje, where the Spanish Battalion was stationed and there I met Mr. Alber Benabou [phoen] who was the head of the office for information and he informed the United Nations on what was going on. In Medjugorje --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour we should stop here because we have a lot of names now and they are not in the transcript. Maybe my learned colleague will ask the question again about the names of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Our witness was dealing with at that period of time because they are not in the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think during the testimony the -- it should be in the form of question and answer, rather than the narration by this witness himself. And we missed the names in the transcript. Mr. Seric, would you please ask some questions as for those names so that we could have it correctly registered in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, you heard this warning and the objection by my learned friend. Please look my way. Let me help you, because this Tribunal is not like tribunals in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Croatia. Everything needs to be translated and recorded, and if it is recorded in the way you said it, then we will achieve some result. Then your testimony will make sense. However, if your words are not recorded as they should be, then your arrival here is not in vain but it will not be as effective as it would be if your words are recorded properly. Please curb yourself a little, slow down a little, and as Mr. President has just warned you, I have now been rather fast but let me ask you to repeat the names, look at the transcript, and see that the names are recorded just the way you say them. You mentioned Vlado Soljic and others. I don't want to lead you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Mr. Vlado Soljic was Defence Minister in Herceg-Bosna. I worked with him for a short while but for a much longer time, it was Mr. Perica Jukic. He was the defence Minister of Herceg-Bosna, who had his headquarters in Posusje. I went to him to ask him to give me a pass for East Mostar and he gave me the pass. Before that, I gave approvals by Mr. Pero Pusic, who was the head of the office for the exchange of prisoners of war in Mostar. I used this pass to go to the Spanish Battalion and he -- they submitted my request to the East Mostar. In the East Mostar, Mr. Safet Orucevic, and I don't know what his position was at the time, Sisic Rusmir and Smail Klaric, who was the mayor of Mostar, some of them submitted the request. I can't see the names in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 72, row 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Who is the mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the East Mostar, during the war, in 1993, the mayor was Smail Klaric, and his deputy was Rusmir Cisic. And in the West Mostar, at the time, I believe that the mayor was -- he is currently the principal of the school of education.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter absolutely didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, did you make rounds of the detention centres in the West Mostar and in the East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I made rounds of the detention centres, first in the East Mostar, I visited my comrades who used to work with me, Mr. Slachko Sesar, Dr. Vlaho, I paid a visit to them, to see how they were. I had a chat with them, and after that, I visited in the West Mostar, I visited the Heliodrom several times. I was in Dretelj once. I was in Ljubuski once. I couldn't really go to Ljubuski. Ljubuski was very inaccessible because it was under the control of the political instances directly reporting to Mate Boban but in East Mostar I must have entered the prison more than ten times. In the East Mostar, I visited the detainees on the wish of their parents who contacted me. I brought them packages. I brought them dressing materials, medicines. There was a lad there whose last name was Ratkovic, and I can't remember his first name, who had been wounded and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who was dressed by Dr. Vlaho all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have to wait a little bit. Yes. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also visited the hospital in the East Mostar, as well as the hospital in the West Mostar, and on one occasion, I was appointed as the President of the council of the hospital, that's when Dr. Lang came to Mostar, to East Mostar, and to Nova Bila to West Mostar. And the West Mostar at the time the health minister of Herceg-Bosna was Dr. Ivan Sarac. The head of the medical services was Dr. Ivan Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you please slow down for the record? You may continue.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I described the situation in the East Mostar to them. I told them that there were thousands of shells falling there and that over 60 of their shells fell on the hospital, that the children are very thin there, undernourished, that there were no medicines and the two of them, together with Dr. Sandrk who was there at the time, expressed their humanity and they told me that all the drugs that I -- that they needed they would give to me to take to them. The doctors who were in the East Mostar at the time, it was Zlatko Sisic, Dr. Milavic, whatever they asked for I would bring to the hospital to them. In addition to that, I tried to -- I will stop if you want me to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: No, just slow down.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: In addition to that, I tried to help some patients by bringing them a token present such as a chocolate bar, a facial cream for a blond girl who had lost her leg. After the end of the war, as a token of my gratitude, I took Dr. Ivan Sarac to Israel to visit my wife, who lives there, and we visited Israel together. I saw that people wanted to live together and that could clearly be seen after the end of the war in 1994, when we organised the humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have problems. What the witness is saying and what is written is two different things. He said that Dr. visited his country, Israel and that his wife lives there. Can he clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have painted a picture for us in the courtroom, especially for the Trial Chamber, and the whole -- this whole story that you have told us, can you tell us what Vinko Martinovic represented to you? What was he to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I told you that the Jewish community in Mostar is an institution and for that reason, we worked only with those who were on the top of the government. Stela, who was at the time a soldier, he was the leader of a unit, he didn't represent anything to us, especially not a reliable partner so we did not see the need to turn to him for a simple reason. I didn't expect any help coming from him. It is possible that if any of the Jews had been incarcerated in any of the detention centres outside, such as the Heliodrom or the Dretelj, I would have turned to him, but fortunately, nobody was there and we didn't have any problems, and for that reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What places are you talking about? If somebody had been incarcerated then you would have turned to him for help. Can you please wait for me to finish my question, sir? I don't understand what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to say. If any of the Jews had been, for example, imprisoned at the Heliodrom, I would have turned to Slobodan Bozic. If any of the Jews had been found -- had been missing and had not been at the Heliodrom, I would have paid a visit to all the ATG units to see if that person was there. So if anything had happened, I would have turned to him. So if -- I'm not saying that he was running any of the camps but I would turned to him. That's what I'm saying. And thank God this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. I have brought my direct examination to an end. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, I am a trial attorney and I will ask you some questions which are stemming from the examination-in-chief by your counsel. So you keep -- now you still keep the position of the president of the Jewish society of Mostar, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum, did you happen to have any contacts with a representative of international organisations, such as ECMM, Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I've had contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you make any official statements to them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Throughout the entire war, shall I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but very briefly, please. My question was very brief.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: During the war, I had contacts with all the organisations starting with Mr. Mazowiecki, who came to Mostar in 1995 and 1996 with the Red Cross with the High Representative --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not of your nationality or Croat nationality so I don't understand the language you're speaking so I need sometime for the translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Mandelbaum I notice you have to wear glasses to read and I think you take them off when you're looking around. If you look, if you put your glasses on and you look at the monitor, there is a little black dot there and that indicates that the translation has completed. Now, unfortunately, you'll have to keep your glasses on but if you just follow the progress of that dot, we won't have to keep interrupting you, because believe me what you say is extremely valuable to this Tribunal because you're one of the very few people who is a native of Mostar but who wasn't involved in the conflict. So would you bear that in mind? We really want to hear what you have to say. It's important for Mr. Martinovic and it's important for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I think most of the questions require a simple answer, that is yes or no. If the Prosecution would like to pursue it on that direction, he will ask you more questions about it. If you have something to explain to us, just do it in a very concise way. Mr. Prosecutor, would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you make any official statements which were relevant to your activities as a president of the Jewish society and the situation in Mostar and the whole Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Jewish population?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I did not issue any statements but on several occasions, I spoke to all the representatives, the High Representative, the Red Cross and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: My next question will be: Is it correct that there were 2200 Jews in the whole Bosnia-Herzegovina and 1.000 of them left? During the war, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: This could be correct, because today in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are 995 Jews living.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what was the reason why the Jewish population had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Economic reasons. People were afraid of war. They didn't know what to expect. The year 1941 was still fresh in the memory of a lot of people. In addition to that, a number of people left Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time because they thought, and they expected, that the war would last only three or four months, like in Croatia. I said Jews were not expelled from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Very few of them were imprisoned. And they lived just like all the other citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina and they lived in the areas inhabited by the majority population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct, Witness, that your Jewish community, and you as the President of the Jewish community, tried to -- just to have a neutral position in this armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Not that we tried, but we managed to do that. The only convoys carrying food and medicines coming to Mostar were Jewish convoys. Except for those sent by Europe via the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like, Mr. Usher, to show the witness Exhibit 796.3. It's an ECMM report. It's in English but if you allow me, I can read it and with the assistance of the interpreter, maybe Mr. Mandelbaum can explain some things which may derive from this statement. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: This will be page 2 of this document, and item 222.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Can you please translate this? I can't read English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, may I read a part of this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: "We met Zoran Mandelbaum, head of the Jewish community in Mostar yesterday, he said, "Jews were the first to provide aid to Mostar in 1992 through the Jewish non-governmental organisation"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It says "East Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: "Non-governmental organisation "La Beno Valencia." They still provide help to all three sides. Jews are neutral in this conflict, with a wish and programme to live in a unified Mostar. Jews of Mostar are completely assimilated, often mix-married. There were 2200 Jews in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war. 1.000 have left. Most of them are old and retired people." Witness, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Is it your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who it was given to but I must have spoken to somebody because I had a lot of excerpts from papers, American papers, Dutch papers, and I have a tape here, taped by Annette Basalel [phoen]. She is the director of the Dutch television. So I would be happy if you watched this because it features the citizens of Mostar. It -- maybe it would give you the impression of the situation as it was in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandelbaum. Maybe the Trial Chamber will make such kind of decision.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So Mr. Mandelbaum, there were already problems during the Serb aggression in Mostar, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Absolutely. When the Serb aggression on Mostar started, or rather the JNA, we did not know what would befall the Jews, whether we would also be the object of the aggression or whether it would only be the Croats and the Muslims who were together at the time, they fought side by side, and embraced similar idea, just as it happened in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you first saw Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela, in the period when there was a Serb aggression in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Absolutely. I did not know him before the war. I had never seen him. And when I went to see him, it was absolutely the first time that I had laid my eyes on him. I've already explained the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No need to repeat just your statement, your testimony. Did you have an impression that Mr. Vinko Martinovic was a sort of commander? Because you were directed to him.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Absolutely. Vinko Martinovic enjoyed the authority, and he was a commander because behind him there were three men standing, and behind me there were also three men standing. Even though he was casually dressed and barefoot, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was he a HOS commander at that time or commander of some other unit when you saw him first?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Yes. He was a HOS commander. I mean it was common knowledge in Mostar. I never asked him to see any papers, but everybody said that Stela was the HOS commander and that he was number 1 there. It was a semi-private unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what about 1993? During the military conflict between the ABIL and HVO, do you know what position did Mr. Vinko Martinovic occupy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: No, I don't think I could tell you that. I know that at that time I used to see his men. I never came across him during the conflict in 1993 and 1994. It was only when the conflict was over that I went to see him, and that is when I saw him, with a professor of the Rome, University of Rome who wanted to write a book who had come to write a book about Mostar. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's stop at that. So you just told the Trial Chamber that you saw Mr. Martinovic people. What do you mean by that? And where did you see his people in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I used to see his men in the streets of Mostar, on Avenija, I saw them walk up and down. Because you see, Mostar is a small town. In Mostar, you know who slaps whom and when. Let alone such things. And I could see those people because they behaved very arrogantly and their insignia were somewhat different than those of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And why did you know that they were Stela's people or Vinko Martinovic's people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Well, I knew it because I used to see them, in 1992, at the headquarters and standing watch in front of the military hospital where his headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You just told the Trial Chamber that they behaved somehow arrogantly. Do you know what kind of reputation did they have in Mostar in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: In 1993, as before that, those men were, how shall I call it, local mobsters, local gangsters, you never knew what they might spring on you or what they might do at any point in time. They -- they had some daily schedules, they sat around, I never sat down with them, but I used to see them in the restaurant there in those coffee bars there along the Avenija, where they would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And they continued to behave in this same way in 1993, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: Listen, I didn't see them harm anyone. Let me tell you that, right from the beginning. I did not see that but one could see how boisterous, how arrogant they were and from that one could conclude that they felt as the real authority there, but when we would be bringing in the humanitarian aid, never once did they try to prevent the passage of the humanitarian aid on where we loaded the trucks, when people which -- the parcels, that is, which people in West Mostar were sending to their friends on the east side. They never stopped it and even once a van came driven by one of his combatants and they had prepared some ten parcels or so for their people. I must say I feared that perhaps there were explosives in them but thank God it all went fine. I never dared of course asked them what they were sending and to whom they were sending them. Had they wanted to or rather had Stela wanted to, he could have prevented the complete humanitarian action of the Jewish community in Mostar. On one occasion, though, we did have a problem but it did not originate with Stela. It was with another commander, the commander of the civilian police at a checkpoint, where the separation line was. And then I had to -- to ask the late President Tudjman for help and after that it was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that those soldiers, I mean Vinko Martinovic's soldiers, had a lot of power. What did you mean by that? Power over the population of West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: I believe they had powers, not from the official -- not granted to them, not conferred upon them by the official authorities but because they had taken the power in their own hands. I think that the police could have very little say because everybody was armed. There was a curfew so that one never knew who could do what.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you just testified today that the expulsion of Muslims in Mostar started on the 20th of April. Who started the expulsion of Muslims on the 20th of April in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: The HVO. Listen, the Muslims and Croats, in all units, and the same goes for Stela's unit, were the majority. I'm referring to the foot soldiers. The commanders were Croats. When the expulsions started on the 20th of April, it was done under the pretext that they had come from east Herzegovina, from Nevesinje, from Gacko, they had taken Serb flats, so that Croats from -- who had come from Bosnia had no where to live. And for that reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm satisfied with your response to my question now. And my second question will be now: You also testified that the mass expulsion of Muslims started after the 9th of May, and who performed that mass expulsion of Muslims from Mostar -- West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MANDELBAUM
utterances.text: The HVO. As a matter of fact, on the -- after the 9th of May, soldiers came to my house. They came and they were masked and I guess that those two who had come from it my place they were not from Mostar I'm sure about that. Where they had come from I have no idea but they had HVO uniforms with some red arm bands and they had their faces painted and they were for instance those who expelled people. I was staying with my mother. She was 92 years old and she was afraid. From the house where she lived, all Muslims of a younger age were expelled, only those who could not move on their own were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we still have five minutes to go but since there will be re-examination and Judges' questions, we decided to stop here. Witness, I'm afraid that you have to come back tomorrow because we have not finished your testimony yet. As I did to other witnesses, I have to warn you that during your stay in The Hague, you are still under the oath. So do not talk to neighbour about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, fully, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
